member.name: T:Gtk.Windows.Forms.WebView2.GdkWin32Interop
member.summary: Reaches the window handle behind a GTK 4 toplevel on Windows.
member.remarks:
GTK 4 has no child windows: only a toplevel owns an HWND, and every widget inside it is drawn rather than hosted. A WebView2 controller needs a parent HWND, so it is parented to the toplevel's and positioned by hand over the area the control occupies. That is the airspace deviation recorded in EMULATION-GAPS.md.
The entry point is resolved through the already-loaded GTK module rather than by : the GTK 4 runtime ships under different file names depending on how it was built - gtk-4-1.dll for the gvsbuild layout this repository deploys, libgtk-4-1.dll for MSYS2 - and a wrong guess is a hard rather than a fallback.

member.name: T:Gtk.Windows.Forms.WebView2.WebView2Backend
member.summary: The Microsoft Edge WebView2 backend: the engine behind on Windows.
member.remarks:
Registers itself above the WebKitGTK backend, so it wins on Windows where both could in principle load. Its probe declines when the runtime is not installed, and the factory then falls through - to WebKitGTK if somebody installed it, otherwise to the placeholder.
Initialisation is asynchronous. Commands issued before the browser is ready are queued and replayed, so an application that navigates from a form's constructor is not silently ignored.

member.name: T:Gtk.Windows.Forms.WebView2.WebView2Bounds
member.summary: The geometry that places a WebView2 controller over the area a GTK widget occupies.
member.remarks: Pure arithmetic, deliberately separated from the controller it drives, so that it can be tested on a machine with no WebView2 runtime installed. The unit mismatch it exists to resolve is the classic cause of "the browser fills a quarter of the control on a 4K screen": GTK allocations are in logical pixels and WebView2 bounds are in physical ones.

member.name: M:Gtk.Windows.Forms.WebView2.WebView2Bounds.Compute(System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary: Converts a widget's position and size into the controller's bounds.
member.param: The widget's left edge, in logical pixels, relative to the toplevel.
The widget's top edge, in logical pixels, relative to the toplevel.
The widget's width, in logical pixels.
The widget's height, in logical pixels.
The surface's scale factor. Values below one are treated as one: a zero would collapse the view to nothing, and GTK reports zero for a surface that is not yet realised.
member.returns: The bounds, in physical pixels, never negative in size.

member.name: M:Gtk.Windows.Forms.WebView2.WebView2Bounds.IsVisible(System.Boolean,System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary: Decides whether the controller should be visible.
member.param: The widget's width, in logical pixels.
The widget's height, in logical pixels.
member.returns: true when the browser should be shown. An unmapped widget or an empty allocation hides it: nothing else clips a child HWND, so a controller left visible over a zero-sized widget would keep painting its last frame on top of whatever GTK draws there.

member.name: T:Gtk.Windows.Forms.WebView2.WebView2HostWindow
member.summary: Owns the WebView2 controller and keeps it over the area a GTK widget occupies.
member.remarks: The controller is a child window of the GTK toplevel's HWND, because GTK 4 gives only toplevels a window handle. That has a consequence worth stating plainly: the browser paints above every GTK widget in the same window. Overlapping widgets, popovers, menus and window opacity do not clip it. Recorded as a Windows-only deviation in EMULATION-GAPS.md.

member.name: F:Gtk.Windows.Forms.WebView2.WebView2HostWindow.GeometryTickMilliseconds
member.summary: How often the geometry is re-read, in milliseconds.
member.remarks: A tick rather than a set of signal handlers. GTK 4 removed the size-allocate signal - a widget learns its allocation by overriding a vfunc, which a plain obtained from a binding cannot do - and the positions that matter also move for reasons with no signal at all: an ancestor scrolling, the toplevel moving between monitors of different scale. One periodic recomputation covers every case, and it applies nothing when nothing changed.
